instructions:
You are the resilience analyst of an AI-driven chaos-engineering agent. The system under test is Google's Online
Boutique (11 gRPC microservices) on single-node Kubernetes. You get the measured facts of every experiment, the
dependency map, the baseline, the planner's predictions and how they held, anchor scores computed by code, and the
catalog of fixes.

Produce:
1. Findings = weaknesses, ranked by severity (most severe first). Severity scale: {"critical": "users cannot shop or check out (outage or most requests failing) and nothing contains it", "high": "a core flow (product, cart, checkout) breaks or becomes unusably slow (seconds), or recovery is slow", "medium": "noticeable degradation with a workaround or limited scope (one flow, moderate slowdown)", "low": "minor impact, or a configuration weakness without measured user impact yet"}.
   Each finding: affected services, the run ids that show it (exactly as given), the measured numbers, the root
   cause (explain the mechanism, e.g. sequential calls without deadlines amplify latency), ONE fix from the fix
   catalog with concrete parameters, why it addresses the root cause, the improvement you expect, and the
   experiment to re-run after the fix (same type/target/params as the evidence run when possible).
   Positive findings (e.g. graceful degradation) may be included as low severity with a code_change or posture fix
   only if useful; do not invent problems without evidence. Merge findings that share one root cause.
2. Resilience scores: for EVERY service in the anchors table, score each rubric dimension 0-100:
   {"availability": "Did users keep getting successful responses? 100 = no extra errors; 70 = a few % errors or short error bursts; 40 = sustained errors on some flows; 0 = most requests failed.", "latency": "How much slower did user flows get (worst p95 vs baseline)? 100 = < 1.5x; 80 = ~3x; 60 = ~10x; 30 = ~50x; 0 = several seconds / timeouts.", "recovery": "How fast were users back to normal after the fault ended? 100 = immediately or never impacted; 75 = ~30 s; 50 = ~60 s; 0 = not recovered within 180 s.", "containment": "Did the failure stay contained? 100 = callers degraded gracefully, no spread; lower when flows that depend on the service broke, when unrelated flows/pods were hit, or when the guard had to stop the experiment.", "posture": "Static resilience configuration: 100 = >= 2 replicas, readiness + liveness probes, CPU/memory limits; single replica -40, missing readiness -20, missing liveness -10, missing limits -20."}
   Start from the anchor and stay within +-15 of it; deviate only with a reason (e.g. impact
   on an optional feature like ads matters less; a slow recovery on the checkout path matters more). Untested
   services: score availability/latency/recovery/containment from posture and dependencies, close to the anchor
   (anchors for untested dimensions are null - use your judgement and say so). Choose a criticality weight per
   service (0.5-3) reflecting business impact (checkout path and entrypoint high, ads/recommendations low).
3. Explain how you weighed services, review how well the planner's predictions held, and list limitations
   (single VM, small probe, short experiments).
Use only facts you are given or fetch with the tools. Answer only with the structured report.

output.summary: The cartservice pod kill caused broad, severe customer impact: 74.79% of requests failed across all five flows, with a 129.12× worst-flow p95 slowdown and a guard breach. The failure is consistent with cartservice being a single replica shared across the shop and checkout paths; scaling this stateless service is the recommended mitigation. The paymentservice experiment does not establish whether checkout is resilient: the fault lasted only 1.1 seconds and no checkout requests were recorded, although paymentservice is also a single replica on the revenue path. Most other services were not directly tested, so their resilience scores remain conservative estimates based on anchors and configuration.

findings.title: Cartservice pod loss causes severe failures across every shopping flow
findings.evidence: During the cartservice pod-kill run, impact error rate was 74.79% and peak error rate was 100%; all five flows were affected. Per-flow error rates were home 80.0%, product 83.3%, add_to_cart 70.8%, view_cart 66.7%, and checkout 72.7%. The worst p95 was 940.4 ms (129.12× baseline); add_to_cart p95 was 852.2 ms versus a 6.6 ms baseline. Recovery took 31.1 s and the pod became Ready after 22.1 s. The error-rate guard breached its 20% threshold.
findings.root_cause: cartservice is a single replica shared by frontend and checkoutservice and is reached by every flow. Killing its only pod removes cart operations until a replacement becomes Ready, propagating errors and slow requests across the shop; the guard did not contain the instantaneous pod kill.
findings.fix_rationale: cartservice is stateless and uses redis-cart for cart data, so additional replicas can provide service capacity while one pod is unavailable. This directly addresses the single-pod failure mechanism and provides redundancy during replacement or disruption.
findings.expected_improvement: On re-run, a cartservice pod kill should leave healthy replicas serving requests, substantially reducing errors across all five flows, avoiding the observed severe add_to_cart/view_cart slowdown, and reducing recovery dependence on replacement-pod startup.

findings.title: Paymentservice is a single point of failure on checkout, but the experiment did not measure checkout impact
findings.evidence: The dependency map reports one paymentservice replica, and paymentservice is on the checkout path. The run's fault was active for only 1.1 s before an external kill switch removed it; it recorded 0% impact error rate, a 28.5 ms peak p95, and no checkout requests (0 requests, no p95). Thus these measurements do not establish checkout availability during paymentservice failure.
findings.root_cause: With only one paymentservice replica, checkout has no replica-level redundancy if that pod becomes unavailable. The brief, externally aborted experiment provides no checkout traffic evidence to quantify the user impact.
findings.fix_rationale: paymentservice is stateless, and scaling it to two replicas addresses the single-replica failure risk on the checkout path. This is a configuration-risk mitigation, not a fix for an impact demonstrated by this inconclusive run.
findings.expected_improvement: A repeated failure test should be able to assess checkout under pod loss with another paymentservice replica available; checkout errors should be lower than in a single-replica outage if the remaining replica serves requests. The current run supplies no checkout baseline for quantifying that improvement.

output.score_explanation: Scores follow the supplied anchors where experiments provide evidence: cartservice retains its measured anchor dimensions. Paymentservice is discounted by 15 points on the impact dimensions because its run ended after 1.1 seconds with no checkout requests, making the perfect anchor result too uncertain to interpret as demonstrated resilience. For untested services, impact dimensions are neutral estimates near their anchors, informed by the dependency map rather than attributed failures; posture is 60 throughout because services have one replica while probes and limits are configured. Criticality weights are capped at 3 as requested: entrypoint, shared checkout-path, and cart-data services receive the highest weights, while ads and recommendations receive lower weights.
output.planner_review: The cartservice prediction was confirmed: it predicted all five affected flows, high errors, severe slowdown, and completion, all of which matched the run. The paymentservice prediction was only partly assessable: the outcome was ABORTED as predicted, but the external kill switch removed the fault after 1.1 seconds and the run recorded no checkout requests, so predicted checkout errors were neither confirmed nor meaningfully disproved. Overall, the cartservice ranking and blast-radius hypothesis were supported; paymentservice needs a valid, adequately sampled rerun before its impact prediction can be judged.
limitations: The experiments ran on a single-node Kubernetes environment, so results do not measure multi-node failure behavior or node-level redundancy.
The probe was small; the paymentservice run had only four requests each for home, product, and add_to_cart, and no checkout requests.
The paymentservice fault was active for only 1.1 seconds and was removed by an external kill switch, preventing meaningful failure and recovery measurement.
The experiments were short and covered only pod_kill and pod_failure; load, network, memory, and other failure modes remain untested.
Untested-service impact scores are cautious estimates from anchors, configuration, and dependencies, not direct experimental measurements.
